#en:
I keep telling myself the hum of the reactors is comforting, but tonight it just sounds like teeth grinding in the dark. PX-2395 feels wrong lately. Not dangerous in any clear way, just out of tune, like a grav ring a few RPMs off. Maybe it is just me. Maybe I am just tired.

We ran another inspection loop over the aft systems, Jonah Kincaid cracking the same bad jokes he always does about SysDef not paying him enough to climb into access trunks that smell like boiled suit liners. Marcus Hale laughed, but the sound caught halfway, like his throat had forgotten how. He snapped at Jonah later in the mess when the coffee ran out, slammed the mug so hard it chipped. Jonah went quiet, stared at the table. Nobody said anything until Sara Holloway changed the subject to a card game. Marcus apologized after, mumbled something about not sleeping. We all pretended that was enough.

Elena Marquez sat through all of it, that unreadable half-smile on her face. She has been like that more and more, hovering on the edge of conversations, not quite in them. When I asked if she was all right, she said she was just "processing the latest directive" and changed the topic to training rotations. That is the thing with Elena. She always has the right words, but lately they land a little too clean, like they were rehearsed.

Mira Chen stopped me in the corridor outside life support this morning, eyes red, hands shaking. Her brother on Jemison has some kind of respiratory issue, and the last comm burst from home said the waiting list for treatment is longer than the time his doctor says he can afford. Mira cried, really cried, chest-heaving, gasping sobs she kept trying to smother because "SysDef does not break." I held her till she stopped shaking. Later, Elena passed us and asked if there was "a situation." I said no, everything was fine. That was a lie and we all knew it.

I keep thinking about my mother back in New Atlantis, stuck in that tiny apartment looking at the same patch of sky where Earth used to matter. Her last message mentioned "a little stiffness" that she brushed off, but I saw the way she moved her hand, how slow it was. If it gets worse, I am half a system away locked on deployment. I tell myself I signed up to protect people like her, that this distance means something. Then I remember how long it took us to respond to the last piracy report and wonder if that is true or just what we need to believe so we can sleep.

There is talk in the lower decks that some of our "abandoned" targets are not accidents at all, that ships like this one get left to drift on purpose when the politics get messy. Jonah said he heard at Gagarin Landing that a whole refit line got written off because "the numbers had to look a certain way" for a board back on Jemison. He laughed when he said it, but it did not reach his eyes. I file all of that under rumor, but rumor has teeth out here.

I am starting to understand that if I wait for some perfect day to feel happy, it will never come. Between patrol logs and emergency drills and the soft, constant threat of being in the wrong place when somebody cuts a maintenance corner, there is not a lot of room for joy. Still, when Mira made a joke about us all retiring to a beach somewhere that does not exist, I laughed hard enough my stomach hurt. For a minute, I felt like I deserved to laugh, like all the nights cataloguing faults and double-checking seals might entitle me to something gentle someday. It felt strange, daring, almost wrong, to think I might deserve that.

Part of me also wonders if I deserve whatever is waiting out here, good or bad. I have moved my share of reports to the bottom of the stack when it was easier. I have looked away when an order felt more convenient than just. Maybe that is just how the system works, and I am complicit. Maybe the universe does not keep score. But when the lights flicker just a fraction too long, when the hull creaks like a tired joint, I catch myself thinking, if something happens, did we earn it.

Tomorrow I am running another calibration check with Elena. She requested me specifically, said she "trusted my eye for detail." I should feel flattered, I guess. Instead I feel that little murmur of unease you get when a bulkhead reads within spec but your fingertips swear the metal is too warm. I keep telling myself it is nothing. That the truth behind all of this is simple: long hours, thin nerves, too much space and not enough answers. But there is a part of me that wonders if we are all just making it convenient to ignore what is really cracking under the paint.
zh:
我一直告诉自己反应堆的嗡鸣让人安心，可今晚它听起来像在黑暗中磨牙。PX-2395 近来不对劲。不是任何明显的危险，只是走调，像一圈重力环比该有的转速差了几个 RPM。也许只是我。也许我只是累了。

我们对后部系统又跑了一遍检查环，乔纳·金凯德照常讲着他那些关于星防队给他的薪水不够爬进闻起来像煮过的宇航服内衬的检修通道的烂笑话。马库斯·黑尔笑了，可声音在半途卡住，像他喉咙忘了怎么笑。后来在食堂咖啡喝完时他冲乔纳发火，把杯子砸得那么重，磕掉了一块。乔纳安静下来，盯着桌子。直到萨拉·霍洛韦把话题换成打牌才有人说话。马库斯事后道歉，嘟囔着没睡好。我们都假装那够了。

埃琳娜·马尔克斯全程坐着，脸上那种难以读解的半个微笑。她越来越常这样，悬在谈话边缘，不太进得去。我问她还好吗，她说她只是在"处理最新指令"，然后把话题换到训练轮换。埃琳娜就是这样。她总有对的话，可近来它们落地时太干净，像排练过。

今早米拉·陈在生命维持系统外的走廊拦下我，眼睛通红，手在抖。她在杰米森的弟弟有某种呼吸问题，而家里来的最后一次通讯突发说治疗的等待名单比他医生说他能负担的时间还长。米拉哭了，真的哭了，哭得胸口起伏、抽气般地哽咽，她一直努力压住，因为"星防队不会垮"。我抱着她直到她不再发抖。后来，埃琳娜路过我们，问是不是"有情况"。我说没有，一切都好。那是谎话，我们都清楚。

我总想起我在新亚特兰蒂斯的母亲，困在那间小公寓里，望着地球曾经要紧的那同一片天空。她最后一条消息提到"有点僵"，一带而过，可我看见她活动手的方式，有多慢。要是恶化了，我在半个星系之外、锁在部署中。我告诉自己我入伍是为了保护像她这样的人，说这段距离有意义。然后我记起我们花多久才回应上一次海盗报告，于是怀疑那是真的，还是只是我们需要相信、好让自己能睡着的东西。

下层甲板有传言说我们某些"被遗弃"的目标根本不是事故，说像这样的船在政治变复杂时会被故意留在那儿漂。乔纳说他在加加林着陆点听说一整条改装线被注销，因为杰米森某个董事会需要"数字看起来某种样子"。他说这话时笑了，可那笑没到眼睛。我把那些都归进传言，可传言在这外面有牙。

我开始明白，如果我等着某个完美的一天去感到幸福，它永远不会来。在巡逻日志、紧急操练、以及有人抄维护近路时你恰好在错的地方的那种轻柔而持续的威胁之间，没有多少留给快乐的空间。不过，当米拉开玩笑说我们都要退休去某个不存在的海滩时，我笑得肚子都疼了。有那么一分钟，我感觉自己配得上笑，像所有那些编目故障、复核密封的夜晚有朝一日也许配得上一点温柔。那感觉很陌生、很大胆，几乎不对——觉得自己也许配得上那个。

我身上一部分还想知道，我是否配得上在这外面等着的一切，好或坏。当那样更省事时，我也把我那份报告挪到堆底过。当一道命令感觉比公正更方便时，我也移开过目光。也许系统就是这么运转的，而我是同谋。也许宇宙并不记分。可当灯多闪了那么一丝、当船壳像疲惫的关节一样吱嘎时，我发觉自己在想：要是出了事，是我们挣来的吗。

明天我要和埃琳娜再做一次校准检查。她特意要了我，说她"信任我对细节的眼力"。我大概该觉得受宠若惊。结果我感到的是当一面舱壁读数在规格内、可你指尖却发誓金属太热时那种小小的不安低语。我一直告诉自己那没什么。这一切背后的真相很简单：长工时、神经紧绷、太空太多而答案不够。可我身上有一部分想知道，我们是不是都在图方便地忽视那在漆面底下真正开裂的东西。

#en:
Could not sleep again, so I am burning power on this pad instead of staring at the ceiling of the berth and counting the weld seams.

Today was simple on paper. Perimeter sweep, sensor recalibration, live-fire drill in bay three. The usual Outpost Nightwatch routine, where everything is squared away, logged twice, and no one ever admits they are tired. Darius runs the line like he was born with a rifle welded to his shoulder. Elena moves through a room like a ghost, calls her shots before she takes them. Watching the two of them on the range, you would think this outfit is clean, sharp, uncomplicated.

Then you step off the firing line and everyone goes silent when the door to the briefing room opens.

We do not ask who paid for tonight's contracts. We just see the data packet, the route overlays, the "non-attributable" clause stamped in the corner. Marcus pretends he does not notice those seals, but I catch him flicking his eyes to them every time. Professional curiosity, he calls it. I call it a survival instinct. Men like us do not live long if we stop asking who benefits when the gun smoke clears.

Rumor in the mess is that one of our recent clients has their hands deep in frontier food shipments, moving more than manifests say they do. Darius says that is above our pay grade, to keep our noses in our own optics and out of corporate ledgers. Elena does not say anything, but she always takes her tray to the far table lately, back to the wall, eyes on the door. You can tell when a job brushes too close to something she has seen before. She gets that stillness, like she is waiting for an echo.

We ran escort last week on a convoy nobody wanted to talk about. Crates with the serials shaved down, cold-storage humming louder than it should, and a route that bent wide around any major hub. I asked the handler if we were hauling medical, he said "nutrients" and changed the subject. Since then, half the unit swears they saw dust signatures in the distance that did not match any of our own. Someone riding the weather, watching us without wanting to be seen. Might be nothing. Might be someone testing how close they can run alongside our paymasters without us noticing.

Outpost Nightwatch has unspoken rules. You do not ask where the money comes from. You do not freeze your teammate out, no matter how much you want to. You do not miss a shot that matters. Break the first two and the work stops coming. Break the last and men like Darius and Elena cannot trust you on their flank. Trust is rationed out here more carefully than air.

I keep thinking about that when the generators dim at night and the humming settles into something almost like quiet. About how much of what we do is built on the idea that the floor will stay under our feet as long as we follow orders and keep our optics clean.

But I have seen floors give way.

I keep coming back to that station, years ago, when I was still green. Alarms screaming, bulkheads shaking like they were alive and trying to tear free. I had her in my arms, the only calm point in a corridor full of panic. She was laughing and crying at the same time, blood on her teeth, insisting she could walk even as the deck pitched under us. We held on to each other while the lights went out and the world sounded like it was tearing apart around us. Love and loss, tangled so tight I still cannot pull them apart in my head. By the time the noise stopped, she was gone and the corridor was just another twisted passage on a casualty report.

Since then, every contract feels like a slow replay of that moment. Different walls, different clients, same question rattling around in my skull. How much of this is going to come down on our heads, and who am I going to be holding when it does.

Outpost Nightwatch likes to act like we are above the places we work. Private, disciplined, detached. The truth is we live in the same air as everyone else. If these whispers about shipments and scorched farm belts are true, then whatever is turning soil sour out there will not stop at a perimeter line. It will find its way into our vents, our water, our mess trays.

For now, the ops board is full, the pay hits on time, and the only things we are allowed to kill are what show up on the briefing slides. Darius trusts the numbers. Elena trusts her instincts. Marcus trusts patterns in the intel that nobody else has noticed yet.

Me I am trying to decide if I still trust the outpost more than I trust the feeling in my gut that we are walking the edge of another collapsing corridor, waiting to see who we will be holding when the lights go out.
zh:
又睡不着，所以我烧电力写这块数据板，而不是盯着住舱天花板数焊缝。

今天纸面上很简单。外围扫描、传感器重校、三号舱实弹操练。照例的前哨夜巡流程，一切收拾利落、记录两遍、没人承认自己累。大流士带队像他生来肩上就焊着一支步枪。埃琳娜像鬼一样穿过房间，开火前先报自己的弹。在靶场上看着他们俩，你会以为这支部队干净、锋利、不复杂。

然后你走下射击线，每次简报室的门一开，所有人都安静了。

我们不问是谁付了今晚的合同。我们只看到那个数据包、航路叠层、角落里盖着的"不可归属"条款。马库斯假装没注意那些印，可我逮到他每次都把眼睛瞟向它们。职业好奇，他这么叫。我叫它求生本能。像我们这样的人一旦不再追问枪烟散去后谁得利，就活不长。

食堂里的传言说我们最近某个客户的手深插在边疆粮食运输里，运的比清单说得多。大流士说那超出我们的薪资等级，叫我们把鼻子管在自己的光学件上、别伸进企业账簿。埃琳娜什么都不说，可她近来总把托盘端到最远的桌子，背靠墙，眼睛看着门。你能看出什么时候一份活儿擦得太靠近她见过的东西。她会变成那种静止，像在等一道回声。

上周我们给一支没人想谈的运输队做护航。序列号被磨掉的箱子、比该有的更响的冷藏嗡鸣，以及一条绕开任何主要枢纽的宽阔航线。我问那办事员我们是不是在运医疗品，他说"营养品"，然后换了话题。从那以后，半个部队赌咒说他们在远处看见尘埃特征，和我们自己的任何东西都对不上。有人骑着天气，看着我们却不想被看见。也许没什么。也许有人在测试他们能多靠近我们的金主而不被我们注意。

前哨夜巡有不成文的规矩。你不问钱从哪儿来。你不把队友冷落在外面，无论你多想。你不打丢要紧的一枪。破前两条，活儿就不来了。破最后一条，像大流士和埃琳娜这样的人就无法在侧翼信任你。在这外面，信任比空气还省着分配。

当夜里发电机变暗、嗡鸣沉进某种几乎像安静的东西时，我总想起这个。想起我们做的有多少建在"只要听命令、保持光学件干净，地板就会一直在我们脚下"这个念头上。

可我也见过地板塌陷。

我总回到那座空间站，多年前，我还青涩时。警报尖叫，舱壁像活的、要挣脱一样摇晃。我把她抱在怀里，是满走廊恐慌里唯一平静的点。她同时笑着哭着，牙上有血，坚持说自己能走，哪怕甲板在我们脚下倾覆。灯灭时我们互相抓着，世界听起来像在我们四周撕裂。爱和失去缠得那么紧，我至今在脑子里分不开。等噪声停下时，她已经不在了，而那条走廊只是伤亡报告上又一条扭曲的通道。

从那以后，每一份合同都像那一刻的慢速重放。不同的墙、不同的客户，同一个问题在我颅骨里回响。这些有多少会砸到我们头上，而当它砸下来时我会抱着谁。

前哨夜巡喜欢表现得凌驾于我们工作的那些地方。私密、守纪、抽离。事实是我们和所有人呼吸同样的空气。如果这些关于货运和烧焦农田带的低语是真的，那么外面那让土壤变酸的东西不会停在一条外围线前。它会找到路钻进我们的通风口、我们的水、我们的食堂托盘。

眼下，行动板上排满了，薪水准时到账，我们被允许杀的只有简报幻灯片上出现的那些。大流士信任数字。埃琳娜信任自己的直觉。马库斯信任情报里还没被别人注意到的图案。

而我——我在试图决定，我是否仍信任前哨胜过信任我肚子里那个感觉：我们正走在又一条正在塌陷的走廊边缘，等着看灯灭时我们会抱着谁。

#en:
I used to mark time in survey windows and burn limits. Thirty seven minutes over the pole, ninety to grab atmosphere reads, three hours to convince some overworked clerk on Queue Row that the numbers did not justify delaying a hundred people's lives another year. Now I mark it in how often I have to move the ship before someone notices the gaps I left in their records.

The first crack was not dramatic. No one fired a shot. I filed a risk assessment on a little rock with too much dust in the air and not enough water under the ground. The models said marginal, high failure chance with the prefab kit they were budgeting. I wrote all of that down. I watched the board stamp it "pending." Next month I saw the same coordinates come back through as "revised, approved" with my risk section overwritten by someone who had never set foot outside an office. Six months later I listened to the distress calls taper off from that place, the way the signal starts clean, then ragged, then just static. Officially, that outpost was "lost due to unforeseen conditions." Unforeseen, my ass.

People think I ran for profit. Some of it is credits, sure. Spacers will pay for a line that does not end in a waiting room. Settlers on their last shot will pay for a valley that has not already been promised to three different corporations. But the real reason I fled the nice clean desk was the day I realized I had become the excuse for other people's shortcuts. My name under approvals I did not write, my models cited to justify landings I would never have signed off on. Either I scrubbed myself out of that machine, or I let it keep eating people in my handwriting.

Hearthline was the one I cannot stop circling, even out here. Early job, early mistake. On paper it was my model that greenlit it. In my memory, I never cleared it. Somewhere between those two truths is a file someone erased and a radio log I still hear when I am too tired to keep the noise out. That is the day "safe enough" stopped sounding like anything but a lie.

So I built something else in the margins. A network of almost worlds and hidden valleys, places I had run numbers on and then watched get buried under "administrative complexity." I started selling what the queues would never reach. One family here, three ships there, coordinates slipped across a bar in Neon's Underbelly or whispered beside a rusted gantry in Akila. Every time it worked, it felt like stealing something back from the people who thought they owned the grid. Every time it failed, I added another waveform to the archive and told myself I would do better next time.

They say I am dying. Maybe. Radiation is not a rumor. Some days my hands shake when I draw a nav line, and the cough tastes metallic. Healing, if you can call it that, has started to feel like nothing at all. There are mornings I wake up and the guilt is not clawing at my ribs, and for a second I wonder if that is progress or if I have just gone numb enough to function. Numb enough to move the next group, adjust the next manifest, pretend the archive of lost signals is just data and not voices I knew by name.

This canyon I am in now was always supposed to be the last experiment. Kade's Pocket, they started calling it when I was not listening. The numbers are right water, shelter, decent soil, tight approach vectors easy to hide in shipment noise. I routed just enough cargo here to keep them alive without drawing a straight line any idiot could follow. It made sense as a final proof of concept a place the big powers could not revoke with a signature. If I can get this one truly self sustaining, truly off every chart, then maybe all the compromises and corpses in my wake add up to something other than a crime.

What I am afraid of is not the bounty hunters or the suits sniffing around my old logs. It is that someone will crack the pattern and decide to copy it without the hesitations. No risk models, no sleepless nights over weather anomalies, just raw throughput. I bent the grid to feed people I thought the system was throwing away. There is nothing stopping someone else from bending it to make themselves king of a valley they did not earn.

So I keep moving between the canyon and the junkyards, between the farmers who swear they owe me everything and the brokers who know exactly how much my head is worth. I keep hoarding transmission ghosts and half erased jump plans, telling myself that if I can just finish this one hidden settlement, just once get everyone in and stable and safe, then maybe I will have earned the right to lie still long enough to feel something other than this thin, dangerous calm.
zh:
我以前用勘测窗口和点火限度来标记时间。极点上方三十七分钟，抓大气读数九十分钟，花三个小时说服排队区某个累坏的文员相信这些数字不构成再把一百个人的生活推迟一年的理由。如今我用得挪动这艘船多少次、才不至于有人注意到我在他们记录里留下的空白来标记时间。

第一条裂缝并不戏剧性。没人开枪。我对一块大气里灰尘太多、地底下水太少的小岩石提交了一份风险评估。模型说边缘，用他们预算的预制套件失败概率高。我把那些全写下来了。我看着董事会把它盖成"待定"。下个月我看见同样的坐标以"修订、批准"回来，我的风险部分被某个从没踏出办公室的人覆盖了。六个月后我听着那个地方的求救呼叫渐渐稀少——信号先干净、然后破碎、然后只剩静电。官方上，那座前哨"因未预见的情况而失联"。未预见，我的屁股。

人们以为我逃走是为了利益。有些是信用币，当然。太空人会为一条不终结在候诊室的航线付钱。最后一搏的定居者会为一个还没被许诺给三家不同企业的山谷付钱。可真正让我逃离那张干净办公桌的，是我意识到我已成了别人抄近路的借口的那天。我的名字在被批准的、我没写的档下面，我的模型被引用来为那些我绝不会批准的着陆背书。要么我把自己从那台机器里擦掉，要么我让它继续用我的笔迹吃人。

炉线是我停不下来绕着转的那个，即便在这外面。早年的活儿，早年的错误。纸面上是我的模型给它放行的。在我记忆里，我从没批准过它。在这两个真相之间的某处，有一份被人擦掉的文件，和一段我太累到挡不住噪声时仍会听见的无线电日志。就是那天，"足够安全"开始听起来除了谎言之外什么都不是。

于是我在页边建了别的东西。一张由几乎世界和隐藏山谷构成的网，那些我算过数字、然后眼看被埋在"行政复杂性"底下的地方。我开始出售那些队列永远不会触及的东西。这里一家人，那里三艘船，坐标在霓虹城下层的酒吧里滑过、或在阿基拉一根锈蚀吊架旁被低语。每次它奏效，感觉像从那些以为拥有这张网的人手里偷回了什么。每次它失败，我就往档案里加一段波形，告诉自己下次会做得更好。

他们说我快死了。也许。辐射不是传言。有些日子我画航线时手会抖，咳嗽尝起来是金属味。愈合，如果你能这么叫的话，开始感觉什么都不是。有些早晨我醒来，愧疚不再抓挠我的肋骨，有那么一秒我想这是进步，还是我只是麻木到能运转了。麻木到能挪动下一批人、调整下一份清单、假装那档案里的失落信号只是数据，而不是我按名字认识的声音。

我现在待的这个峡谷本该是最后一个实验。我不在听时，他们开始叫它凯德的口袋。数字是对的——水、掩体、像样的土壤、紧到容易藏在货运噪声里的进近矢量。我改道了刚好够的货物到这里，让它们活着而不留下任何白痴都能跟的直线。作为一个最终的概念验证说得通——一个大国无法用一纸签名撤销的地方。要是我能让这一个真正自给、真正脱离每一张星图，那么也许我一路留下的所有妥协和尸体加起来就是别的什么，而不是一桩罪行。

我害怕的不是赏金猎人或在我旧日志周围嗅探的西装。而是有人会破解这个图案、决定不带犹豫地照抄它。没有风险模型，没有为天气异常失眠的夜晚，只有生的吞吐量。我掰弯这张网是为了喂那些我认为系统在抛弃的人。没有什么能阻止别人掰弯它，去让自己成为一座并非他们挣来的山谷之王。

所以我在峡谷和废料场之间不断移动，在那些赌咒说什么都欠我的农民和那些确切知道我脑袋值多少钱的经纪商之间。我继续囤积传输幽灵和半擦除的跃迁计划，告诉自己：只要我能建完这一座隐藏定居点、就一次让所有人都进去、稳定、安全，那么也许我就挣到了停下来久到能感觉到别的什么的权利，而不是这份稀薄、危险的平静。
